lead: Two shops can have the same standard deviation and still differ in risk if their average sales differ. The coefficient of variation divides the spread by the mean, so series in rupees, kilograms or marks can be compared on one scale. The Lorenz curve draws cumulative income against cumulative households and turns inequality into an area. Skewness reports which tail of a distribution is longer; kurtosis reports how heavy the tails and peak are. Together they describe spread and shape before any test or regression.
prereq: You need: mean, median and mode and standard deviation and quartiles.

blocks.text: The standard deviation has the same unit as the data. A spread of ₹60 looks large beside a mean wage of ₹120 and small beside ₹6,00,000. The coefficient of variation (CV) removes the unit and the scale:

blocks.where: SD is standard deviation; mean is arithmetic mean; both in the same unit; CV is a percentage with no unit. The mean must be positive.

blocks.text: A small CV means values sit close to their mean, so the series is more consistent. CV is used to compare wages, rainfall, share prices and quality scores. See 1.3 for SD.

Income inequality is spread across people, not around a mean. Order households from poorest to richest. The Lorenz curve plots cumulative percentage of income against cumulative percentage of households. The line of equality joins (0,0) to (100,100); every household then has the same income. A real curve bows below it because poorer households hold less than their population share.
Gini = 2 × area between line of equality and Lorenz curve
blocks.where: For n equal groups, G = 1 − (1/n) Σ [F(i−1)+F(i)]; F(i) is cumulative income proportion at group i, F(0)=0. G=0 is perfect equality. G=1 is the limiting case of infinitely many households where one takes all; with n equal groups the grouped formula tops out at 1 − 1/n (0.8 for five groups), so the computed Gini is a slight understatement for small n.

blocks.text: A flat start and steep end means many low incomes and a few high incomes: right-skewed.

Skewness measures asymmetry. In a symmetric distribution mean = median = mode. A long right tail gives mean > median and positive skewness; a long left tail gives mean < median and negative skewness. Karl Pearson's coefficient is
Sk = (mean − mode)/SD, and for moderately skewed data use the equivalent form 3(mean − median)/SD, which avoids needing the mode.
blocks.where: SD is standard deviation. The median form is used when mode is unstable. Sign gives direction; |Sk| > 1 suggests strong skew.
Q₁ and Q₃ are first and third quartiles. It lies between −1 and +1 and resists outliers.

blocks.text: Kurtosis measures peak and tail weight. With central moments m₂ and m₄,

blocks.where: m₂ is variance and m₄ is the fourth central moment. Normal: β₂=3, γ₂=0 (mesokurtic). γ₂>0: leptokurtic, heavier tails; γ₂<0: platykurtic, lighter tails. Only a few universities teach the moments-based versions at this stage.

figure.caption: The Lorenz curve bends below the line of equality; the wider the gap, the more unequal the incomes.

spec.aria: A Lorenz curve bowing below the diagonal line of equality, with the gap between them widest in the middle.

examples.question: (a) Factory A: mean wage ₹520, SD ₹60. Factory B: mean wage ₹680, SD ₹72. Which is more consistent? (b) Five equal household groups receive 5%, 10%, 17%, 23% and 45% of total income. Find cumulative shares, the Lorenz points and the Gini coefficient. (c) For a city, mean income ₹24,000, median ₹21,000, SD ₹9,000. Find Karl Pearson's skewness and name the tail.
steps: CV of B = 72/680 × 100 = 10.588...% ≈ 10.59%. B has the smaller CV, so B is more consistent.
Skewness = 3(24000−21000)/9000 = 3×3000/9000 = 1.0. Positive, so the tail is on the right and mean > median.
examples.answer: B is more consistent (CV 10.59% vs 11.54%); Gini = 0.372; skewness = +1.0, a right tail.
examples.check:
a_mean, a_sd = 520, 60
b_mean, b_sd = 680, 72
print(round(b_sd / b_mean * 100, 2))
print(round(a_sd / a_mean * 100, 2))
shares = [5, 10, 17, 23, 45]
cum = []
s = 0
for x in shares:
    s += x
    cum.append(s / 100)
gini = 1 - (1/5) * sum(((cum[i-1] if i > 0 else 0) + cum[i]) for i in range(5))
print(round(gini, 3))
print(round(3 * (24000 - 21000) / 9000, 1))

traps: CV has no unit; never compare it with an SD or add it to one.
Bowley's coefficient uses the median; the denominator is Q₃ − Q₁, not SD.
Positive skew means the longer tail is on the right, so mean > median.
A Gini of 0.372 is a pure number between 0 and 1; written as a percentage it is 37.2%. Never write 0.372%, and never attach a unit to it.
Normal has β₂ = 3 and excess γ₂ = 0; β₂ = 0 is not mesokurtic.

quiz.q: Define coefficient of variation and give its unit.
quiz.a: CV = (SD/mean)×100; it is a percentage with no unit.

quiz.q: Why can CV compare two SDs in rupees while SD cannot?
quiz.a: CV divides SD by the mean, removing the unit and scale; raw SD depends on scale.

quiz.q: Mean = 80, SD = 12. Find CV. A second series has mean 100, SD 10. Which is more consistent?
quiz.a: CV = 12/80×100 = 15%; second CV = 10%; second is more consistent.

quiz.q: Q₁ = 20, median = 28, Q₃ = 40. Find Bowley's coefficient and its sign.
A Lorenz curve is flat for the first 70% of households, then rises steeply. What does this say about income shares and skewness?
quiz.a: Poorest 70% get a small share; top 30% get most; right-skewed.

quiz.q: Mean = 50, median = 56, SD = 8. Find 3(mean−median)/SD and name the tail.
β₂ = 4.2. Find excess kurtosis and classify.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same idea appears in finance as the Sharpe ratio, which divides the average excess return (average return minus the risk-free rate) by the SD of returns. Note it is the CV turned upside down: return per unit of risk instead of risk per unit of return. Gini coefficients guide tax and subsidy debates. Skewness and kurtosis feed risk models because heavy tails make rare losses more likely. Search for 'Lorenz curve Gini coefficient' and 'excess kurtosis' for data-lab practice.
